Exploratory Data Analysis of the Titanic Disaster¶

CodeAlpha Data Analytics Internship - Project: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Objective¶

Understand who survived the sinking of the Titanic and why, using a structured EDA workflow:

# Step Where
1 Ask meaningful questions about the dataset before analysis Section 1
2 Explore the data structure, variables and data types Section 2
3 Identify trends, patterns and anomalies Section 3
4 Test hypotheses and validate assumptions using statistics and visualisation Section 4
5 Detect potential data issues to address in further analysis Section 5
6 Conclusions, limitations and next steps Section 6

Dataset: 891 passengers x 12 variables (the Titanic training split; see data/DATA_DICTIONARY.md). Tools: Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn.

In [1]:

                         cramers_v, rank_biserial, cohens_d, effect_label, iqr_fences)

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="notebook")

1. Ask meaningful questions before analysing¶

On 15 April 1912 the RMS Titanic sank after hitting an iceberg; 1,500+ people died. Lifeboat capacity was limited, so who got a place was not random. Before touching the data, I write down what I want to learn.

Guiding questions¶

ID Question Why it matters
Q1 What does the dataset contain, and is it trustworthy (types, missing values, errors)? Every later conclusion depends on data quality
Q2 Who was on board? (age, sex, class, family, port) Context for interpreting survival
Q3 What was the overall survival rate? Baseline to compare groups against
Q4 Did sex, class, age, family size or port of embarkation relate to survival? Core of the analysis
Q5 Is fare informative on its own, or just a proxy for class? Separates correlated drivers
Q6 Do factors interact (e.g. sex x class)? Are some patterns confounded? Avoids misleading headline numbers
Q7 Which data problems must be fixed before modelling? Prepares the next stage

Hypotheses to test (stated before looking at results)¶

ID Null hypothesis (H0) Planned test
H1 Survival is independent of sex Chi-square test of independence
H2 Survival is independent of passenger class Chi-square test of independence
H3 Fare has the same distribution for survivors and non-survivors Mann-Whitney U (fare is skewed)
H4 Age has the same distribution for survivors and non-survivors Mann-Whitney U (+ Welch t-test as sensitivity check)
H5 Survival is independent of port of embarkation Chi-square test of independence
H6 Survival is independent of family group (alone / small / large) Chi-square test of independence

Assumptions I will validate¶

  • Normality and equal variances (decide parametric vs rank-based tests)
  • Expected cell counts >= 5 for chi-square tests
  • Independence of observations (passengers who share a ticket travelled together, so this may be violated)
  • Multiple testing: six primary hypotheses -> Bonferroni correction (alpha / 6)

Data dictionary and measurement levels¶

The dtype pandas assigns is not always the statistical type: Survived and Pclass are stored as integers but are binary and ordinal respectively, and PassengerId is just an identifier.

What the structure tells us¶

  • 891 passengers, 12 columns: 5 integer, 2 float (Age, Fare) and 5 text columns. The target Survived is balanced enough for analysis: 342 survived (38.4%) and 549 did not.
  • Mis-typed variables: Survived (binary), Pclass (ordinal) and PassengerId (identifier) are integers but must not be treated as continuous numbers.
  • Missing data: Cabin is missing for 687 rows (77.1%), Age for 177 (19.9%), Embarked for only 2.
  • Skew: Fare is extremely right-skewed (mean 32.2 vs median 14.5, maximum 512.3, skewness 4.79), whereas Age is roughly symmetric (mean 29.7, median 28). SibSp reaches 8 and Parch 6, so some very large families exist.
  • Name is unique for each passenger but embeds a title (Mr, Mrs, Miss, Master...), a useful hidden feature.

3. Identify trends, patterns and anomalies¶

First I derive a few exploratory features from existing columns (the full cleaning pipeline is in Section 5).

In [9]:
eda = df.copy()
eda["Outcome"] = eda["Survived"].map(LABELS)

# Title from name; merge spelling variants; group rare titles
eda["Title"] = eda["Name"].str.extract(r",\s*([^.]+)\.", expand=False).str.strip()
eda["Title"] = eda["Title"].replace({"Mlle": "Miss", "Ms": "Miss", "Mme": "Mrs"})
eda["TitleGroup"] = eda["Title"].where(eda["Title"].isin(["Mr", "Mrs", "Miss", "Master"]), "Rare")

# Family
eda["FamilySize"] = eda["SibSp"] + eda["Parch"] + 1
eda["FamilyGroup"] = pd.cut(eda["FamilySize"], [0, 1, 4, 20], labels=["Alone", "Small (2-4)", "Large (5+)"])

# Age / fare bins
eda["AgeGroup"] = pd.cut(eda["Age"], [0, 12, 18, 35, 60, 100],
                         labels=["Child (<=12)", "Teen (13-18)", "Adult (19-35)", "Middle (36-60)", "Senior (61+)"])
eda["LogFare"] = np.log1p(eda["Fare"])
eda["FareQuartile"] = pd.qcut(eda["Fare"], 4, labels=["Q1 (lowest)", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4 (highest)"])

# Cabin
eda["HasCabin"] = eda["Cabin"].notna()
eda["Deck"] = eda["Cabin"].str[0].fillna("Unknown")

eda[["Name", "Title", "TitleGroup", "FamilySize", "FamilyGroup", "AgeGroup", "Deck"]].head()

plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "02_univariate_distributions.png", FIG); plt.show()

Observations

  • The ship was male-dominated (577 men vs 314 women, 65% men) and 55% of passengers travelled third class (491).
  • Most people embarked at Southampton (644), and most travelled alone (SibSp = 0 for the majority).
  • Age is unimodal with a small bump of infants and children; Fare is heavily right-skewed - the log(1 + Fare) transform brings the skew from 4.79 down to about 0.39 and is the better scale for analysis.

3.2 Overall survival and the four headline factors¶

In [11]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(18, 4.8))

counts = df["Survived"].value_counts().sort_index()
axes[0].bar(["Did not\nsurvive", "Survived"], counts.values, color=[C_DIED, C_SURV], edgecolor="white", width=0.6)
for i, v in enumerate(counts.values):
    axes[0].text(i, v + 8, f"{v}\n({v / len(df):.1%})", ha="center", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 680); axes[0].set_ylabel("Passengers"); axes[0].set_title("Overall outcome")

rate_bar(axes[1], df, "Sex", order=["female", "male"], title="Survival rate by sex")
rate_bar(axes[2], df, "Pclass", order=[1, 2, 3], title="Survival rate by class", xlabel="Passenger class")
rate_bar(axes[3], df, "Embarked", order=["C", "Q", "S"], title="Survival rate by port", xlabel="Port (C / Q / S)")
fig.suptitle("Dashed line = overall survival rate (38.4%)", fontsize=11, y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "03_survival_overview.png", FIG); plt.show()

Observations

  • Only 38.4% of passengers survived overall.
  • Sex is the strongest pattern: 74.2% of women survived vs only 18.9% of men - a four-fold gap.
  • Class gradient: 63.0% (1st) -> 47.3% (2nd) -> 24.2% (3rd).
  • Cherbourg passengers survived most often (55.4%) vs Queenstown (39.0%) and Southampton (33.7%) - but see Section 4.3, where I check whether this is a real port effect or a class effect in disguise.

3.3 Interaction: sex x class¶

In [12]:
rate = df.pivot_table(index="Sex", columns="Pclass", values="Survived", aggfunc="mean")
n = df.pivot_table(index="Sex", columns="Pclass", values="Survived", aggfunc="count")
annot = np.array([[f"{rate.iloc[i, j]:.0%}\n(n={n.iloc[i, j]})" for j in range(rate.shape[1])]
                  for i in range(rate.shape[0])])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
sns.heatmap(rate, annot=annot, fmt="", cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=0, vmax=1, linewidths=2,
            cbar_kws={"label": "Survival rate"}, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Survival rate by sex and class"); ax.set_xlabel("Passenger class"); ax.set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "04_sex_class_heatmap.png", FIG); plt.show()

Observation - sex and class interact. Women in 1st and 2nd class almost all survived (96.8% and 92.1%), but third-class women survived only half the time (50.0%). Men did badly everywhere: 36.9% in 1st class, but just 15.7% and 13.5% in 2nd and 3rd. Looking at sex or class alone hides this structure.

            palette={"female": "#c44e8f", "male": "#4c72b0"}, seed=SEED, ax=axes[2])

axes[2].set_ylabel("Survival rate"); axes[2].tick_params(axis="x", rotation=25)

print("Mean age - survivors: %.1f | non-survivors: %.1f" % (
    eda.loc[eda.Survived == 1, "Age"].mean(), eda.loc[eda.Survived == 0, "Age"].mean()))

Mean age - survivors: 28.3 | non-survivors: 30.6

Observations

  • The two age distributions overlap heavily (mean 28.3 for survivors vs 30.6 for non-survivors) - age alone is a weak predictor.
  • The visible effect is at the extremes: children aged 12 or under survived 58.0% while passengers over 60 survived only 22.7% (n = 22, so treat with caution).
  • Splitting by sex reveals the "women and children first" pattern: boys (56.8%) fared almost as well as girls (59.4%), but from the teenage years men's survival collapses (roughly 9-19%) while women's stays at 75% or more.

3.5 Fare and wealth¶

In [14]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 4.8))

sns.boxplot(data=eda, x="Pclass", y="LogFare", color="#dd8452", ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_ylabel("log(1 + Fare)"); axes[0].set_xlabel("Passenger class"); axes[0].set_title("Fare by class (log scale)")

sns.kdeplot(data=eda, x="LogFare", hue="Outcome", palette=PALETTE, common_norm=False, fill=True, alpha=0.35, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_xlabel("log(1 + Fare)"); axes[1].set_title("Fare distribution by outcome")

rate_bar(axes[2], eda, "FareQuartile", title="Survival rate by fare quartile")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "06_fare_analysis.png", FIG); plt.show()

print("Median fare by class:", df.groupby("Pclass")["Fare"].median().round(2).to_dict())

Median fare by class: {1: 60.29, 2: 14.25, 3: 8.05}

Observations

  • Fare tracks class closely (median fare 60.29 in 1st, 14.25 in 2nd, 8.05 in 3rd class).
  • Survival climbs steadily with fare: 19.7% -> 30.4% -> 45.5% -> 58.1% from the cheapest to the most expensive quartile.
  • Because fare and class are so entangled (Spearman rho = -0.69), Section 4 tests whether fare adds information within a class.

3.6 Family, title and cabin¶

In [15]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(18, 4.8))
rate_bar(axes[0], eda, "FamilyGroup", title="Survival rate by family group")
sizes = sorted(eda["FamilySize"].unique())
rate_bar(axes[1], eda, "FamilySize", order=sizes, title="Survival rate by exact family size")
rate_bar(axes[2], eda, "TitleGroup", order=["Mr", "Master", "Miss", "Mrs", "Rare"],
         title="Survival rate by title", xlabel="Title (from name)")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "07_family_title.png", FIG); plt.show()

print(eda.groupby("HasCabin")["Survived"].agg(["mean", "count"]).round(3).rename(index={False: "No cabin recorded", True: "Cabin recorded"}))

                    mean  count
HasCabin                       
No cabin recorded  0.300    687
Cabin recorded     0.667    204

Observations

  • Non-linear family effect: passengers travelling alone survived 30.4%, small families (2-4 people) 57.9%, but large families (5+) only 16.1%. Both extremes do worse than the middle. Part of this may reflect the sex and class mix of each group - to be checked in modelling.
  • Title neatly encodes sex, age and marital status: Mr 15.7%, Master (boys) 57.5%, Miss 70.3%, Mrs 79.4%.
  • Passengers with a recorded cabin survived 66.7% vs 30.0% without one. But cabin data is missing for 97.6% of 3rd-class passengers (see Section 5), so HasCabin is mostly a class marker rather than a causal factor.

3.7 Correlation structure¶

In [16]:
corr_cols = ["Survived", "Pclass", "Age", "SibSp", "Parch", "Fare", "FamilySize"]
corr = eda[corr_cols].corr(method="spearman")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6))
sns.heatmap(corr, mask=np.triu(np.ones_like(corr, dtype=bool), k=1), annot=True, fmt=".2f",
            cmap="coolwarm", center=0, vmin=-1, vmax=1, linewidths=1, square=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Spearman correlation matrix")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "08_correlation_matrix.png", FIG); plt.show()

Observations

  • Strongest links with survival: Pclass (rho = -0.34) and Fare (+0.32); FamilySize is weaker (+0.17) and Age negligible (-0.05).
  • Pclass and Fare are strongly (negatively) related (-0.69), and FamilySize is almost a duplicate of SibSp (0.85) and Parch (0.80) because it is built from them -> multicollinearity to handle before modelling.
  • Spearman rank correlation is used because Fare is skewed and Pclass is ordinal. Note that correlation cannot capture the strongly non-linear/categorical effects of sex and family group.

4. Test hypotheses and validate assumptions¶

4.1 Validate assumptions first¶

The choice between parametric and rank-based tests depends on normality and equal variance, so I check these before testing.

In [17]:
age = df["Age"].dropna()
to_check = {"Age": age, "Fare": df["Fare"], "log(1+Fare)": np.log1p(df["Fare"])}

rows = []
for name, s in to_check.items():
    k2, p = stats.normaltest(s)
    rows.append({"variable": name, "n": len(s), "skew": s.skew(), "excess kurtosis": s.kurt(),
                 "D'Agostino K2": k2, "p-value": p, "normal at 5%?": "Yes" if p > ALPHA else "No"})
normality = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("variable")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.5))
for ax, (name, s) in zip(axes, to_check.items()):
    stats.probplot(s, dist="norm", plot=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"Q-Q plot: {name}")
    ax.get_lines()[0].set_markersize(3); ax.get_lines()[0].set_color("#4c72b0")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "09_qq_plots.png", FIG); plt.show()

normality.round(4)

In [18]:
fare_s, fare_d = df.loc[df.Survived == 1, "Fare"], df.loc[df.Survived == 0, "Fare"]
age_s, age_d = age[df.loc[age.index, "Survived"] == 1], age[df.loc[age.index, "Survived"] == 0]

lev = pd.DataFrame({
    "comparison": ["Fare: survivors vs non-survivors", "Age: survivors vs non-survivors"],
    "Levene W": [stats.levene(fare_s, fare_d)[0], stats.levene(age_s, age_d)[0]],
    "p-value": [stats.levene(fare_s, fare_d)[1], stats.levene(age_s, age_d)[1]],
}).set_index("comparison")
lev["equal variances at 5%?"] = np.where(lev["p-value"] > ALPHA, "Yes", "No")

# Chi-square validity: smallest expected cell count
eda["FamilyGroup"] = eda["FamilyGroup"].astype(str)
exp_check = {v: stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(eda[v], eda["Survived"]))[3].min()
             for v in ["Sex", "Pclass", "Embarked", "FamilyGroup"]}
print("Smallest expected count per chi-square test (must be >= 5):",
      {k: round(v, 1) for k, v in exp_check.items()})
lev.round(4)

Smallest expected count per chi-square test (must be >= 5): {'Sex': np.float64(120.5), 'Pclass': np.float64(70.6), 'Embarked': np.float64(29.4), 'FamilyGroup': np.float64(23.8)}

Levene W p-value equal variances at 5%?
comparison
Fare: survivors vs non-survivors 45.0996 0.0000 No
Age: survivors vs non-survivors 1.1954 0.2746 Yes

Assumption check results

  • Fare is strongly non-normal (skewness 4.79) and has unequal variances between survivors and non-survivors (Levene p ~ 3e-11) -> a rank-based test (Mann-Whitney U) is appropriate, not a t-test.
  • The log transform reduces the skew to about 0.39 but, with n = 891, the normality test still rejects (p ~ 2e-9); with large samples these tests flag even small departures, so Q-Q plots matter as much as p-values.
  • Age is mildly non-normal (skew 0.39, p ~ 1e-4) but variances are equal (Levene p = 0.27). Both parametric and rank-based tests are defensible, so I run both and compare.
  • All chi-square tests have every expected count well above 5, so the test is valid.
  • Independence is questionable: 344 passengers shared a ticket with someone else (Section 5), and people travelling together probably shared a fate. p-values are therefore somewhat optimistic.

4.2 Primary hypothesis tests (H1-H6)¶

Effect sizes are reported next to every p-value because with n = 891 even trivial differences can be "significant". p-values are Bonferroni-adjusted for the six primary tests.

In [19]:
M_TESTS = 6   # number of primary hypotheses (Bonferroni)

def chi_test(x, y):
    ct = pd.crosstab(x, y)
    chi2, p, dof, exp = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
    return chi2, p, dof, cramers_v(x, y)

results = []
for hid, label, col in [("H1", "Survival depends on sex", "Sex"),
                        ("H2", "Survival depends on passenger class", "Pclass"),
                        ("H5", "Survival depends on port of embarkation", "Embarked"),
                        ("H6", "Survival depends on family group", "FamilyGroup")]:
    chi2, p, dof, v = chi_test(eda[col], eda["Survived"])
    results.append({"id": hid, "hypothesis": label, "test": f"Chi-square (dof={dof})", "statistic": chi2,
                    "p_value": p, "effect_size": v, "effect_metric": "Cramer's V"})

u3 = stats.mannwhitneyu(fare_s, fare_d)
results.append({"id": "H3", "hypothesis": "Fare differs between survivors and non-survivors", "test": "Mann-Whitney U",
                "statistic": u3.statistic, "p_value": u3.pvalue, "effect_size": rank_biserial(fare_s, fare_d),
                "effect_metric": "Rank-biserial r"})
u4 = stats.mannwhitneyu(age_s, age_d)
results.append({"id": "H4", "hypothesis": "Age differs between survivors and non-survivors", "test": "Mann-Whitney U",
                "statistic": u4.statistic, "p_value": u4.pvalue, "effect_size": rank_biserial(age_s, age_d),
                "effect_metric": "Rank-biserial r"})

res = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("id").reset_index(drop=True)
res["p_bonferroni"] = (res["p_value"] * M_TESTS).clip(upper=1)
res["effect_magnitude"] = res["effect_size"].apply(effect_label)
res["decision"] = np.where(res["p_bonferroni"] < ALPHA, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject H0")
res.to_csv(OUT / "hypothesis_results.csv", index=False)

(res[["id", "hypothesis", "test", "statistic", "p_value", "p_bonferroni", "effect_size", "effect_metric",

               plot_df["abs_effect"], color=colors, edgecolor="white")
for b, v in zip(bars, plot_df["abs_effect"]):
    ax.text(v + 0.01, b.get_y() + b.get_height() / 2, f"{v:.2f}", va="center")

    ax.axvline(x, ls=":", c="grey", lw=1)

ax.set_title("How strongly does each factor relate to survival?\n(green = significant after Bonferroni correction)")
plt.tight_layout(); save_fig(fig, "10_effect_sizes.png", FIG); plt.show()

Results

  • H1, H2, H3, H5, H6 are rejected, even after Bonferroni correction. H4 (age) is not rejected (p = 0.16; rank-biserial r = -0.06, negligible).
  • Effect sizes rank the factors: sex (V = 0.54, large) >> fare (r = 0.38) and class (V = 0.34), both medium > family group (V = 0.29, small and close to medium) > port (V = 0.17, small) > age (negligible).
  • Statistical significance is not the same as importance: port of embarkation is highly significant (p ~ 1.8e-06) yet has only a small effect, and Section 4.3 suggests much of it is explained by class.

4.3 Sensitivity checks and confounding¶

Sensitivity of H4 (age): the Welch t-test gives p = 0.041 (survivors are 2.3 years younger on average) while Mann-Whitney gives p = 0.16. The conclusion flips depending on the test, the effect is tiny (d = -0.16) and p = 0.041 would not survive multiple-testing correction (0.041 x 6 = 0.25). Honest conclusion: no reliable evidence that age alone matters; its role is concentrated among young children and interacts with sex.

# Is fare informative *within* a class, or only a proxy for class?

for c, g in df.groupby("Pclass"):

    within_sex.append({"Sex": sx, "chi-square": chi2, "p-value": p, "Cramer's V": cramers_v(g["Pclass"], g["Survived"])})
print("\nClass vs survival within each sex")
display(pd.DataFrame(within_sex).set_index("Sex").style.format({"chi-square": "{:.1f}", "p-value": "{:.2e}", "Cramer's V": "{:.2f}"}))

Findings

  • Fare is not only a class proxy in 1st and 2nd class: survivors paid more than non-survivors within the same class (1st: median 77.96 vs 44.75, p = 7e-05; 2nd: 21.00 vs 13.00, p = 0.004). In 3rd class there is no difference (p = 0.20).
  • Class matters for both sexes (women p ~ 2e-18, men p ~ 7e-08), so the class effect is not just a by-product of women being over-represented in the upper classes.

Conclusion on H5: the port effect is partly a class effect. Cherbourg's passengers were 50.6% first class (vs 19.7% at Southampton and only 2.6% at Queenstown, where 93.5% travelled third class). Within first class the gap between Cherbourg and Southampton shrinks (69% vs 58%). However, in third class Cherbourg (38%) and Queenstown (38%) still beat Southampton (19%), so class does not fully explain it. The Queenstown first/second-class cells contain just 2 and 3 people, so they cannot be interpreted.

Findings

  • Age (19.9% missing) is not missing completely at random: it is missing much more often in 3rd class (27.7%) than in 2nd (6.0%), and passengers with missing age survived less often (29.4% vs 40.6%, p = 0.008). Dropping those rows would bias the analysis; imputation by group (title x class) is better than one global mean.
  • Cabin (77.1% missing) is informative missingness: missing for 18.5% of 1st class vs 91.3% of 2nd and 97.6% of 3rd class. The raw column is unusable, but the fact a cabin was recorded (and the deck letter) are engineered features.
  • Embarked (2 rows): both are 1st-class women with the same fare (80.0) and cabin (B28); imputing the most frequent port is reasonable for such a small gap.

5.2 Duplicates and independence¶

In [25]:
ticket_size = df.groupby("Ticket")["Ticket"].transform("count")
print(f"Fully duplicated rows        : {df.duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"Duplicated PassengerId       : {df['PassengerId'].duplicated().sum()}")
print(f"Unique tickets               : {df['Ticket'].nunique()} (for {len(df)} passengers)")
print(f"Passengers sharing a ticket  : {(ticket_size > 1).sum()}  (largest group = {ticket_size.max()} people)")
print(f"Survival rate - shared ticket: {df.loc[ticket_size > 1, 'Survived'].mean():.1%}   not shared: {df.loc[ticket_size == 1, 'Survived'].mean():.1%}")

Fully duplicated rows        : 0
Duplicated PassengerId       : 0
Unique tickets               : 681 (for 891 passengers)
Passengers sharing a ticket  : 344  (largest group = 7 people)
Survival rate - shared ticket: 52.0%   not shared: 29.8%

Findings: there are no duplicate rows or IDs, but observations are not independent: 344 passengers shared a ticket with others and these groups survived more often (52.0% vs 29.8%). Group-mates share a fate, so p-values in Section 4 are somewhat optimistic, and any machine-learning model should use group-aware cross-validation (e.g. GroupKFold on ticket) to avoid leakage between train and test folds.

Findings

  • Fare: by the 1.5 x IQR rule, 116 passengers (13%) are outliers (upper fence 65.6). The very highest fares (512.33, paid by three passengers on one ticket) are genuine luxury suites rather than errors, so they are kept and handled with a log transform / robust methods.
  • 15 passengers have Fare = 0: all embarked at Southampton and only one survived. They may be crew, staff or complimentary tickets; this cannot be verified from the data, so they are flagged (not removed).
  • Age has only 11 outliers above the fence (maximum 80) - all plausible.
  • SibSp / Parch: the IQR rule flags 46 and 213 passengers, but it is not meaningful for zero-inflated counts (the fence for Parch is 0 because most people have none). Values up to 8 and 6 are genuine large families, not errors.

12 Dataset Sampling / representativeness 891 of ~2,200 people aboard; training split only Medium Avoid generalising beyond this sample; report as a limitation

5.6 Cleaning pipeline -> analysis-ready dataset¶

Applies the treatments from the issue log and saves outputs/titanic_clean.csv, ready for modelling.

In [29]:
clean = df.copy()

# 1. Embarked: 2 missing -> mode
clean["Embarked"] = clean["Embarked"].fillna(clean["Embarked"].mode()[0])

# 2. Title features
clean["TitleGroup"] = eda["TitleGroup"]

# 3. Age: flag, then impute by median of (TitleGroup x Pclass)
clean["Age_was_missing"] = clean["Age"].isna().astype(int)
clean["Age"] = clean.groupby(["TitleGroup", "Pclass"])["Age"].transform(lambda s: s.fillna(s.median()))

# 4. Family / ticket / cabin features
clean["FamilySize"] = clean["SibSp"] + clean["Parch"] + 1
clean["IsAlone"] = (clean["FamilySize"] == 1).astype(int)
clean["FamilyGroup"] = pd.cut(clean["FamilySize"], [0, 1, 4, 20], labels=["Alone", "Small (2-4)", "Large (5+)"]).astype(str)
clean["TicketGroupSize"] = clean.groupby("Ticket")["Ticket"].transform("count")
clean["HasCabin"] = clean["Cabin"].notna().astype(int)
clean["Deck"] = clean["Cabin"].str[0].fillna("Unknown")

# 5. Fare transform and flag
clean["Fare_log"] = np.log1p(clean["Fare"])
clean["Fare_is_zero"] = (clean["Fare"] == 0).astype(int)

# 6. Drop raw high-cardinality text columns
clean = clean.drop(columns=["Name", "Ticket", "Cabin"])

assert clean.isna().sum().sum() == 0, "missing values remain"
assert len(clean) == len(df)
clean.to_csv(OUT / "titanic_clean.csv", index=False)

before_after = pd.DataFrame({

    "after": [clean.shape[1], int(clean.isna().sum().sum()), clean["Age"].mean(), clean["Age"].median(), clean["Age"].std(), clean["Fare_log"].skew()],
}, index=["columns", "missing cells", "Age mean", "Age median", "Age std", "Fare skew (Fare -> Fare_log)"])

The imputed distribution keeps the overall shape, but filling 20% of rows with group medians adds weight around the middle ages: the median moves from 28 to 26 and the standard deviation shrinks from 14.5 to 13.5. That is the expected cost of median imputation, so models should use the Age_was_missing flag, and results that depend on age should be re-checked on the 714 known ages only. The cleaned file has no missing values and 19 columns.

6. Conclusions, limitations and next steps¶

Answers to the guiding questions¶

Question Answer
Q1 Data quality Clean structurally (no duplicate rows) but with substantial missing Age (19.9%) and Cabin (77.1%), skewed/outlying Fare, zero fares, and non-independent passengers who share tickets.
Q2 Who was on board Mostly men (65%), mostly third class (55%), mostly travelling alone, mostly from Southampton; typical age about 28-30.
Q3 Overall survival 38.4% (342 of 891).
Q4 Drivers of survival Sex is by far the strongest (women 74.2% vs men 18.9%; Cramer's V = 0.54), then class (63% / 47% / 24%) and fare; family group has a non-linear effect (alone 30%, small family 58%, large family 16%); age alone is not a reliable predictor (children are the exception).
Q5 Fare vs class Fare adds information within 1st and 2nd class but not within 3rd class.
Q6 Interactions / confounding Strong sex x class interaction (3rd-class women only 50% vs 92-97% in the upper classes). The port-of-embarkation effect is partly, not fully, explained by class mix.
Q7 Issues to fix See the issue log (Section 5.5): imputation, engineered features, log transform, group-aware validation.

Statistical summary¶

Five of six pre-specified hypotheses (sex, class, fare, port, family group) are rejected after Bonferroni correction; age is not. Effect sizes show that sex >> fare ~ class > family group > port > age.

Limitations¶

  • Observational data: associations are not causal (e.g. class also determined cabin location, which affected escape routes).
  • Sample: 891 of roughly 2,200 people aboard; crew are largely absent.
  • Dependence: group-mates share a fate, so p-values are slightly optimistic.
  • Imputation: 20% of ages are estimated; results involving age should be read with care.
  • Zero fares / missing cabins cannot be verified from the data.

Next steps¶

  1. Fit baseline models (logistic regression, random forest / gradient boosting) on titanic_clean.csv with GroupKFold by ticket.
  2. Include the sex x class interaction and TitleGroup; compare against the simple "women survive" rule as a benchmark.
  3. Examine feature importance and calibration, and check fairness across class and sex groups.
  4. Explore survival within families to understand the large-family penalty.
